chapter: Cal Massey, Coltrane and the Jazztet
title: Cal Massey, Lee Morgan and Philly big-band shows
summary: Tyner and Aisha describe trumpeter Cal Massey, his band and shows around Philadelphia, his friendship with Coltrane, and Lee Morgan's early career.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: You mentioned Cal Massey. Could you talk a little more about Cal because a lot of folks, I know Archie Shepp did a lot of collaborations, “Things Have Got to Change,” things like that. Could you talk a little bit more about him because unfortunately he’s not as-­
He (Tyner) wrote a song for him also once and he recorded it in Japan, called “Folks”.
“Folks” Yeah. We used to call them “Folks” because he acted sometimes older, like an older guy.
But he wasn’t actually that much older than you?
Well, he was older, he was maybe ten or twelve years older.
And he was a trumpet player.
Yeah he was a trumpet player.
He wrote “Nefertiti Suite” and those different tunes . . . His son . . . his wife, Charlotte, they lived in Brooklyn.

Clarence Sharp, we called [him] C Sharp, he played in Cal’s band as well. And then John (Coltrane) and Cal were friends. I’m trying to remember how their relationship came about. I think it was through Naima . . .
I’m not sure how Folks and John met, but they were very close . . .
And so it developed as it did and I had wonderful experiences and I learned a lot over those years. I can’t complain, and meeting John, that was a very historical moment for me.
Well, let’s talk about that meeting-
Everybody says Coltrane, but we say John.
Right.
That’s just like my sister and I called Cal Massey “Folks” and him and John and everybody called him Cal. Lee Morgan was also very close to him.
Lee, that’s right, Lee grew up there as well.
So he was a childhood friend as well, or at least an associate?

Yeah he was like a child prodigy. Lee worked in Dizzy’s band when he was like a kid. He was very mature in that respect, musically, he was a nice guy. Sometimes Dizzy hired him in his band and that was one of his heroes anyway, and then Clifford Brown of course. So it was a very historical city and very artistically rich.
You were asking about Folks, we were close to them when we lived in Long Island and they lived in Brooklyn. In Philly, Calvin put on big shows, Folks, every week, big bands.
He had an entrepreneurial spirit, he liked to put on shows.
In what venues? Where were these shows taking place?
The one in Germantown, I forgot the name of that one, but he’d put them on in Philly at different halls.
Yeah, different places.

You mentioned also that you would perform in house parties and rent parties. What other venues were you doing? Were you doing weddings, were you doing Elks Club or any of those kinds of shows or any of those social clubs . . . high school dances?

I played at some of the Elks Club . . . yeah, I probably did because Cal got a lot of jobs and there were people that would contact him and I was in his band and he was friend of Coltrane, Coltrane was already out, he worked a lot. He started working with Miles of course.
